Ancient navigation

Sight Navigation

The earliest naval navigation consisted of following the coastline, watching
for features on land that would mark their location (landmarks.) When these
navigators lost sight of land, it was very likely they would could not
find land again and would die. When fog came in, they could not sail close
to land or they would run aground; nor could they sail too far from land
or when the fog lifted they would be lost at sea. Also a storm could have
the same effect.

Sailing the latitude

By sighting on the North Star (Polaris), and measuring the angle to it
from the horizon, navigators could tell how far in the north south direction
(latitude) they were. If they knew the latitude of a location and whether
the location was east or west of them, they could sail north or south to
the latitude and then go east or west as required to reach the new location.
This did require occasionally to see the North Star to determine their
latitude and adjust their course accordingly.

At about 150 BCE an instrument called an Astrolabe was invented to measure
the angles and was used to measure the angle to Polaris. It looked like
taking 2 school protractor and fastening them at the center so you would
have a full circle instead of a half circle and putting a sighting rod
pivoting at the center.

Compass

The invention of the compass (believed to be Chinese) allowed these navigators
to sail away from land temporary to get around obstacles (including fog,
reefs, and pirate base) and then know the direction to land. With good
knowledge of the land (shore maps) they could sail out away from land and
still get back. But this did not come into full use until the 1200's. They
used the compass to keep their course to "sail the latitude" when the North
star was not visible (day time, fog, and storms.)

Dead Reckoning

Dead reckoning is predicting your course base on knowledge wind and sea
currents and estimating your direction and speed.

Daring navigators would not
sail directly north or south to the latitude but at an angle so when they
reached the latitude, it was not as far a distance to destination. This
would allow them to go on the hypotenuse instead of traveling the right
angle distances. They had to be careful they would not overshot the location
so they knew whether to sail east or west to the location when they reached
the latitude.

All of this, of course, had to be adjusted base on wind and sea currents.

They would have to estimate their speed and plot on the map how far
they came (using the compass as direction). To estimate their speed, a
man would throw out a log that a rope was tied to and while doing a chant
count how many knots that were on the rope would side though his hands
during the chant or another man would turn a short sand glass and notify
when to stop counting. This would tell them the approximate speed. 
Did
you know the origin of "knots" -- the measurement of speed at sea? 

Another method involved throwing something that floated over board
and do a fast chant while the object floated between two marks on the rail
of the ship.

To measure the time they used "hour glasses" except these where 1/2
an hour in length called "watch glasses". The person who watched the glasses
and turned them as required to keep time was called a "watch" and also
the job and period of time assigned to do the job were all called a "watch."

Did
you know the origin of the word watch meaning the measure of time? And
did you know the origin of the military word "watch" meaning to stand guard?

After
each 1/2 hour, he would ring a bell, one for the first 1/2 hour during
his watch and added a additional one for each subsequent 1/2 hour. After
8 had been done (4 hours), another person would take watch. This gave rise
to telling time by the bells ... 8 bells would be the change of the watch
and it is at 4, 8 or 12 (either AM or PM). One bell is 1/2 hour past the
start of the watch, 4:30, 8:30 or 12:30, etc.

Given the time, speed, and direction they could plot their course fairly
accurately.

Just using this method Columbus
was less than 10% off in his calculations of his position.

Given the sighting of the pole star, they could correct their direction
more accurately.

One of Columbus scientific discoveries was the fact the compass did
not point to true north but deviated the farther he went. He kept this
from the crew, because they were superstitious and he was afraid the crew
would mutiny when they found out that "the laws of God" were being violated.

This is the method that was used in the age of exploration from about
600 AD to 1850 AD.

Stellar navigation

Astrolabe

Stellar navigation is very similar to the Dead Reckoning. The Pole Star,
Polaris, is not always visible. It can't be seen south of the equator nor
when there is haze or fog nor during the day light hours. So the sun and
other stars need to be checked for to determine the latitude.

The instrument called a Astrolabe was invented about 150 BCE by the Greeks
and it had an analog computer on one side to be able to use the sun and
stars other than Polaris to determine the latitude and direction and 
local
time.

The earth revolves on its axis nearly every 24 hours so the sun appears
to revolve around the earth every 24 hours (on the average -- our orbit
is not circular). The sun is directly south (in the northern hemisphere)
every noon (local time). The sun appears to move farther north as summer
approaches and farther south as winter approaches because of the axis tilt.
If you knew how far up in the sky the sun would be at noon and you measured
how far the sun was up in the sky and how long away from noon (time before
noon or after noon) you could compute your latitude. This analog computer
was refined and used by the Arabic Moslems to do this calculation. It was
called by the Europeans "astrolabe" (Greek meaning star taker). The Moslems
needed to know the local time and their location so the would know when
to pray and the direction to Mekka (Mecca) so they knew which direction
to face. See 
Determine Directions with a
Watch 
for an explanation how the time was determined.

The astrolabe has a base that has measurements based on a close approximate
to the latitude. Then it has a plate that slits on top of it that has a
offset circle that represents the path of the sun through out the year.
A rule is set on top of that and with measurements of the location of the
sun to the offset circle, the local time and actual latitude and direction
can be read off the underneath dial. They also added stars as little points
on this plate so they could be used at night.

The other side of this device provided the ability to measure the angles
needed on the front side (the computer side). It could also be used to
measure sine, cosine, and tangent of angles (cotangent of angles over 45
degrees). The first English technical manual, in 1391, was about 
the
Astrolabe (Astrelabie) written by Geoffrey Chaucer
, the same one that
wrote "Canterbury Tales".  The Astrolabe was considered to be the
greatest of all scientific instruments.

European knowledge of the astrolabe and Islamic astronomy originated
in Moslem Spain (Andalusia). The earliest translations of astrolabe material
were in the Christian monastery at Santa Maria de Ripoll. Their translations
were available in Europe by the mid 11th century and were rapidly disseminated.
It is likely that an early carrier of the Arabic translations was Gerbert
of Aurillac (d. 1003) (later Pope Sylvester II - the first French pope).
It is very likely that the adoption of Arabic star names derived from Latin
translations of the star pointers on Islamic (Andalusian) astrolabes. 
This
information came from 
James
E. Morrison who also has Astrolabe web page.
   See his
page for a free computer simulation of an

Astrolabe.

Another instrument called "Gunter's Quadrant" (see at left) was latter
invented that also used to make measurements. Also on the dial face it
had the position of the sun for the dates to allow similar measurements
as the Astrolabe could. The picture shows it got it name because it is
1/4 of a circle The plumb bob is attached what would be the center of the
circle and down one edge is the sights to align it with a star or to let
the sun shine through to a white card to align it with the sun. On its
face there is the path of the sun through the year to allow you to determine
the time and directions like the astrolabe. 
Columbus
tried to use one on his voyages
 to the new world but was unable to
figure it out.

Cross Staff

In the mid 15th century, the Cross staff was invented to measure the angles
more accurately. In a tossing sea, a device such as the astrolabe (and
other measurement devices such as Gunter's quadrant) that depended on a
weight to fix a vertical reference were inaccurate and more so when the
seas were rough. You would be lucky to measure the angle within 5 degrees,
and one degree error puts you off course by 60 knots (90 miles). On land,
however, you could get an fairly accurate measurement.

The
Cross staff used two cross sticks as a sighting device. You sighted the
horizon on the bottom end of the cross stick and moved the cross staff
toward you or farther a way until the top end was on the Pole Star. You
read the angle marked where cross staff meets the main staff. This was
more accurate than the Astrolabe

The Cross staff had some disadvantages. Because you had to see the horizon
and the star at the same time, it could only be used for stars just after
the Sun set or just before the Sun arose.  Another disadvantage was
that you had to be sure to hold it vertical or you would have more error
in the measurement. Still another disadvantage was that at large angles
it was hard to keep both the horizon and the star being measured in sight
at the same time.

Because of each disadvantage both instruments, usually both Astrolabe
and cross staffs were used to take measurements. The calculations were
computed on the Astrolabe.

Sextant

 The
sextant was invented in the 18th century. It allowed you to measure the
angle between the horizon and an object with mirrors. You adjusted the
object's reflection in the mirror so it appears to set on the horizon and
the angle between them is twice the tilt of the mirror. The mirror was
usually offset so when the angle indicator was all the way back it was
at 0 degrees. Also large angles (90 degrees or more) could be measured.
The arc that the scale was on is 1/6 (Latin for six is sex) of a circle
or sextant so all the way forward would tilt the mirror 60 degrees, giving
a measurement of 120 degrees. It did not matter how much the ship was tossing;
as long as you could adjust so the object appeared on the horizon you had
the measurement, even if it was only there for a second.

In general to take a sighting, you set the sextant to 0, aim the telescope
at a star (without the filters) and keeping the star in view adjust the
arm with the moveable mirror until the horizon is in view in the second
half of the mirror, continue adjusting until the image is setting next
to the image of the horizon. The angle from the horizon to the star is
read off the pointer. If you are "shooting" the sun, make sure the filters
are in place.

Accurate tables replaced the analog computer on the astrolabe. It was
hard to get an Astrolabe large enough to handle minutes of degrees much
less seconds of degrees. Because of increase in accuracy of measurements
the sextant gave, you needed large tables to determine you position as
accurate. But the drawback was that you had to have a large book of these
tables which had to be replaced every year to maintain its accuracy. Like
the cross staff, you had to see the horizon and the star at the same time,
it could only be used for stars just after the Sun set or just before the
Sun arose.  To reduce the error of not holding the sextant vertically,
they would rock the sextant back and forth a little to get the smallest
reading.

Longitude

Even with table and sextant you could only accurately place your North/South
distance (Latitude) with accuracy. Something was needed to place your East/West
Distance (Longitude) with accuracy. A great prize was offered for the way
this could be done (20,000 Pounds -- about the equivalent of 2 Million
of today's American Dollars) after a fleet lost in a fog ran aground sinking
4 ships and killing 2000 men because of miscalculated longitude. Many famous
people (like Sir Newton) tried to collect the prize. They tried to use
the moons of Jupiter, but discovered that when Jupiter was on the opposite
side of the sun than the earth, the moons lost time. It was then they figured
the speed of light (based on AU -- Astronomical Units -- units of measure
based on the earth - sun distance). The speed of light was measured long
before the speed of sound.

The longitude problem was solved with an accurate clock. If you could
measure the difference in the local time versus the local time at the places
you left, you could determine the distance east/west. Since the sun appears
to revolve around the earth every 24 hours and there are 360 degrees in
a circle, the time difference multiplied by 360 and divided by 24 would
give the number of degrees East/West from location you left. The British
setup a Naval observatory outside of London in Greenwich and all the measurements
were based its location. Books were published every year that allowed you
to compute the local time and the difference between it and the time at
Greenwich (Greenwich mean time) would give your longitude.

At first every country had its own set of longitude and its own standard
time, but coordination of maps and locations were very confusing between
the countries. It was decided that all naval powers would use one standard.
Since England set the first standard and had the largest naval fleet and
since they had the most charts based on Greenwich, Greenwich was chosen
as the base of longitude measurements. Therefore Greenwich longitude is
0 (called the Prime Meridian) and all time is measured based on Greenwich's
Mean Time -- GMT (now called Universal Time -- UT).

Note: The man who had built the chronograph, Samuel Eliot Morison, could
not collect the 20000 pound prize because the judges wanted something more
like a sextant that could give the correct answer. He got just a portion
of the prize (500 pounds). His children finally collected the rest of the
prize after a long battle.

An introduction to
navigation
 explains how with a digital watch, a sextant, current tables
and a compass, you have all that is needed for celestial navigation.

Reference:

My reference is a 1966 book "American Practical Navigator" sub titled "An
Epitome of Navigation" Published by U.S. Government Printing Office. The
first 30 pages has a history of navigation.  In 1966 it cost $6, pretty
cheap for 1500 pages. I understand that now the book is printed in two
sections. The charts for the year are in a different book. The book is
an excellent reference on how to use, adjust and take care of sextants.
It even has a section on using the "star finder" that shows how to use
a device similar to the Astrolabe to compute your location.  This
book has complete instructions for taking sightings and computing your
location.  It also has a 24 page chapter on "Lifeboat Navigation"
that explains many of the techniques the ancients would use.

Check for these books at

GPS

Now they use GPS (Global Positioning Satellites).  The satellites
know their positions and send a signal with positions and with a time stamp
signal. When a computer gets a measurement from at least three satellites,
it can compute the longitude, latitude, elevation, and time at any position
on the earth.   Simply put, GPS is a bunch of satellites send
out a radio signal that tell you the time the signal was broadcast and
its position.   If you had an accurate timepiece, you use the
time difference to get you distance from the satellite. Light and radio
wave travel at 186,282 miles per hour or 983.294 feet per microsecond (1
millionth of a second).  It will be like you are positioned at some
point in the skin of a ball with the satellite at the center, the distance
from the center of the ball to the skin is determined by time difference
and the thickness of the skin is the error of the clocks. The satellite
clocks are kept in sync to an atomic clock so most the error is in you
instrument.   You do the same with another satellite and you
have another ball determining your position.  Where the two

balls skins intersect, is your position.  The two balls intersection
is a circle, who's thickness and width is determined by the error. 
You do the same the third satellite and where its ball cuts the circle
will be at two points one way out in space and one near the earth (where
you are). The height, width, and length of the points determines by the
accuracy of the clocks.   If you add a forth satellite, its ball
with you position will be slightly off the center of one the points you
calculate, if the time is adjusted so they all add up, you will have the
correct time (near atomic accuracy) and your correct position within a
few meters.

The US government, who launched and controls the satellites, can have
the satellites lie a little about their position or the time they sent
the signals.  If you don't have the codes to know how much they are
lying, your calculations will be off.  It will still be good enough
to navigate, you could be off by a mile but you can't use them to navigate
a missile into a building.   They do this in times of national
emergency.

Clock Numbers

Early history had 12 hours of night and 12 hours of day. This is again
from the 
Babylonians.

12 has may divisors and so you can have rational numbers for 1/2, 1/3,
1/4, and 1/6 of a day. In fact they used a base 12 numbering system. It
has come down to us today in the following forms: 10, 11, and 12 have their
own unique names (not one - teen, etc.); we have words for units of 12
(dozen) and it's next place ( 12*12 = gross) and even the following place
(12*12*12 = great gross). The decimal number 1242 in base 12 is 876 - 8
gross, 7 dozen and 6.

The Babylonians also loved 60 (3*4*5), it is even easier to factor than
12. Also it was magic because of a triangle made of it's lengths was a
right triangle (prove in Pythagorean's theorem 6th century BC), the only
3 consecutive numbers to do so. This is where we get our number of seconds
in a minute and number of minutes in a degree or hour.

The number of degrees in a circle (360 = 3*4*5*6) also came from them
it has more factors than 60.  See below.

Astronomy and Numbers

Everybody know the earth revolves around its axis every 24 hours to give
us our 24 hour day and, therefore, the stars in the sky appear to circle
every 24 hours. 
Almost.
 Because of earth's orbit around the sun,
there is an extra day (24 Hours) in a year. So the are 1 less revolution
around it axis every year than there are days in the year. Therefore the
stars fall a little behind about 4 minutes (24hours / 365.2421988) a day.
At the same time every night, the stars appear to make a backward revolution
every year. Modern star charts, have a calendar around the outside edge
and you set the time of you observation across from the date to give you
a more accurate position of the stars. This correction is 1/365 and since
we adjust the calendar every leap year it is off only about 3 minutes of
time. This error is not noticeable because we use standard time zones and
the local time could be off by about 30 minutes at the edge of a time zone.

In fact the nocturnal has to take it into effect to tell time by the stars.
You line up a "ear" corresponding to the star you are looking at on the
inner circle with the date on the outer circle. Then sighting the pole
star (Polaris) in the center hole, you swing the arm around to the star
you are checking the time with. The arm then shows the time. If you want
to construct your own get the book "Sundials, Their Theory and Construction"
by Albert E. Waugh ISBN 0-486-22947-5 from Dover Publications, a paper
back book costing $5.95 (US). It is available at any book store, although
they may have to order it for you) or at a public library. Or you can buy
the book straight from the publisher -

        Dover Publications
        Dept. 23
        31 East 2nd Street
        Mineola, N.Y. USA 1150

The
Babylonians 
were great astronomers, they noticed that they to adjust
their observations every day also. Also their calendar had 12 months of
30 days and 5 year end holidays giving 365 days a year. It was hard to
compute fractions of 365 (they did not have multiplication or division)
so they used 360 as the number of days for astronomy. They divided a circle
into 360 parts so by setting it back one part every day they could keep
the observations of the stars constant from one day to the next (within
1.5%). The number 360 is 3*4*5*6 which give a great many factors and therefore
great for doing ratios. 
This is where we got 360 degrees in a circle.

Note:
Modern day observers use {1/364.24219889 - .0000000614(t-1900) -- sidereal
time} to adjust their observations. The Babylonians were less than 1.5%
off or about 5 degree per year. This was good since there were no accurate
way to keep time in those days. The would occasionally adjust their based
on the helical rising of certain stars. These are the stars that would
just have risen in the area of the sun when the sun rises.
